issues.legal_issue: A court-appointed receiver may seek the winding up of a debtor company as a means of realizing a debt forming part of the estate under the receiver’s administration.
material_facts: A court appointed a receiver to administer the joint family’s properties, including the unpaid purchase price owed by the company.
The receiver had powers under the court’s order to realize the estate’s assets and debts.
The court later authorized the receiver to file a winding-up petition against the company.
issues.conclusion: The receiver had power to file the winding-up petition to realize the debt due to the estate.
issues.legal_principle: Order XL Rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a court to confer on a receiver powers necessary to realize and manage the estate. Even assuming a winding-up petition is not a suit, the powers relating to realization of property and debts are broad enough to permit such a petition as a form of equitable execution. The court may also confer powers appropriate to the receiver’s administration of the estate. The Court relied on Bowes v. Hope Life Insurance and Guarantee Co., Re General Company for Promotion of Land Credit, and Re National Permanent Building Society.

predicates.receiver_seeks_winding_up_of_debtor_comp: A receiver seeks to have a company wound up as a means of pursuing an estate’s claim against it.
predicates.court_appointed_receiver_administers_est: A court appoints a receiver to administer property belonging to an estate.
predicates.debt_forms_part_of_estate: The debt sought from the company is an asset of the estate administered by the receiver.
predicates.winding_up_can_realize_estate_debt: Winding up the debtor company can serve as a means of realizing the estate’s debt.

issues.definition: When a court-appointed receiver administers an estate that includes a company debt, and winding up can realize that debt, the receiver may file a winding-up petition for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A court-appointed receiver authorized to sue to recover an estate debt is a creditor entitled to present a winding-up petition in respect of that debt.
material_facts: The receiver was appointed to administer the joint family’s properties and was authorized to sue to realize its assets, including the debt owed by the company.
The receiver could demand payment of the debt and, under the court’s authority, could bring an action to recover it in the receiver’s own name.
The receiver presented the winding-up petition based on the company’s unpaid debt.
issues.conclusion: The receiver was a creditor within the meaning of section 439(1) of the Companies Act and was competent to maintain the winding-up petition.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 434 and 439(1) of the Companies Act allow a creditor to initiate winding-up proceedings. A creditor includes a person to whom a debt is payable, including a receiver empowered by the court to sue for that debt. The Court relied on K. V. Mallayya v. T. Ramaswami & Co. and considered In re Sacker and In re Macoun, explaining that a receiver able to maintain an action to recover a debt can be a petitioning creditor.

predicates.receiver_presents_winding_up_petition: A receiver presents a petition seeking the winding up of a company.
predicates.receiver_is_authorized_to_sue_for_estate: The receiver has authority to bring an action in the receiver’s own name to recover a debt belonging to the administered estate.
predicates.company_owes_that_debt: The company owes the estate the debt that the receiver is authorized to recover.

issues.definition: A receiver who presents a winding-up petition is eligible as a creditor when authorized to sue for a debt the company owes to the administered estate.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory demand is not invalid merely because it directs a company to pay the creditor’s debt to a tax authority where that payment discharges the debt and the circumstances leave no feasible alternative security or compromise.
material_facts: A tax authority had directed the company to pay to it the money the company held for the joint family, toward the family’s tax liability.
The receiver’s demand directed the company to pay the amount to the tax authority within the specified period.
Payment to the tax authority would discharge the company’s liability to the joint family.
The demand concerned the full amount directed toward the tax liability, leaving no practical scope for the company to secure or compound the receiver’s claim.
issues.conclusion: The receiver’s demand did not contravene the statutory requirements for a winding-up demand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 434(1)(a) of the Companies Act requires a creditor’s demand and a subsequent neglect to pay, secure, or compound the debt to the creditor’s reasonable satisfaction. The demand need not direct payment personally to the creditor if payment to another person gives the company a full discharge. The opportunity to secure or compound is not an unconditional right where the circumstances do not permit it. The Court referred to Japan Cotton Trading Co. Ltd. v. Jajodia Cotton Mills Ltd., Kureshi v. Argu Footwear Ltd., and W. T. Henley’s Telegraph Works Co. Ltd. v. Gorakhpur Electric Supply Co. Ltd. on the need for statutory demands to comply with the section.

predicates.winding_up_petition_follows_statutory_de: A creditor seeks winding up after serving a demand for payment of a company debt.
predicates.creditor_directs_payment_to_tax_authorit: The creditor directs the company to pay the debt to a tax authority rather than directly to the creditor.
predicates.payment_to_authority_discharges_company_: Payment to the tax authority gives the company a full discharge of its liability to the creditor.
predicates.no_feasible_security_or_compromise_alter: The circumstances do not provide a feasible alternative for securing or compromising the creditor’s claim.

issues.definition: A demand directing payment to a tax authority is not invalid when it follows a winding-up demand, discharges the company’s debt, and no feasible security or compromise alternative exists.

issues.legal_issue: A company neglects to pay a debt after a winding-up demand when it fails to make the demanded payment to a tax authority, even though the debt is subject to a tax collection notice.
material_facts: The tax authority had directed the company to pay the amount it held for the joint family to the authority toward the family’s tax liability.
The receiver’s demand likewise directed the company to pay that amount to the tax authority.
The company did not make the demanded payment.
Making the payment would have complied with the tax authority’s direction and discharged the company’s liability to the joint family.
issues.conclusion: The company clearly neglected to pay the amount within the meaning of section 434 of the Companies Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 434(1)(a) of the Companies Act treats a company as unable to pay its debts when, after a creditor’s demand, it neglects to pay, secure, or compound the debt. In re European Banking Company, Ex parte Baylis was distinguished because there the demand required payment to the creditor despite an attachment that prevented that payment; here the demand required payment to the tax authority, as the tax collection notice directed.

rule.if: winding_up_petition_follows_demand and creditor_directs_payment_to_tax_authority and company_fails_to_make_directed_payment and payment_is_legally_permitted_and_discharges_debt

predicates.winding_up_petition_follows_demand: A creditor seeks winding up after demanding payment of a company debt.
predicates.creditor_directs_payment_to_tax_authorit: The creditor directs the company to pay the demanded amount to a tax authority.
predicates.company_fails_to_make_directed_payment: The company does not make the payment directed by the creditor.
predicates.payment_is_legally_permitted_and_dischar: The directed payment is legally permitted and would discharge the company’s liability for the debt.

issues.definition: A company neglects to pay a debt when, after a winding-up demand directing payment to a tax authority, it fails to make a legally permitted payment that would discharge the debt.

issues.legal_issue: A winding-up petition based on an unpaid debt is not an abuse of process on the ground of a disputed liability when the alleged dispute is not bona fide.
material_facts: The company claimed that the unpaid purchase price was owed to the individual sellers rather than to the joint family.
The family’s manager, who also chaired the company’s board, stated in an affidavit in the partition proceedings that the amount was the balance of the purchase price payable to the joint family.
The Court found that the asserted dispute was not bona fide and formed part of a collusive scheme between the company and the family’s manager.
issues.conclusion: There was no bona fide dispute as to the company’s liability, and the winding-up petition was not an abuse of process on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A winding-up petition cannot be used to enforce a debt that the company bona fide disputes; in that situation, the petition may be an abuse of process. But a dispute that is not bona fide does not prevent the petition from proceeding. The Court relied on W. T. Henley’s Telegraph Works Co. Ltd. v. Gorakhpur Electric Supply Co. Ltd. and In re Gold Hill Mines.

predicates.winding_up_petition_seeks_payment_of_com: A creditor presents a winding-up petition based on a company’s unpaid debt.
predicates.company_alleges_debt_is_disputed: The company asserts that it disputes its liability for the debt.
predicates.alleged_dispute_is_not_bona_fide: The circumstances show that the company’s asserted dispute is not genuine.

issues.definition: When a winding-up petition seeks payment of a company debt, the company alleges a dispute, and that dispute is not genuine, the petition is not an abuse of process on that ground.
